title: Witness and Confession
premise: Wren Thackeray, a night-shift dispatcher who quietly solves the city's small disappearances, takes on the case of Iris Vale, a missing woman whose diary keeps receiving entries after her disappearance. Following the diary's coded references, Wren discovers that Iris faked her death to escape a powerful man who murdered her sister, and that she has been living hidden as a witness preparing to testify. When the man's fixers close in, Wren must choose between protecting his own anonymity and helping Iris bring justice outside a compromised legal system. The story ends with Iris testifying through a recorded confession Wren smuggles to a journalist, toppling the man, while Wren finally steps out of the shadows to claim his own name.
about_author: Mara Dunmore is the pen name of a former emergency dispatcher who spent eleven years listening to a city breathe through a headset before turning those voices into fiction. She writes mysteries about people who live in the margins of official records, and lives somewhere she refuses to disclose.

chapters.title: The Frequency of Missing People
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. On a slow night shift, Wren introduces his off-the-books practice of finding people the police won't look for, guided by taxi radio chatter and city records. A lawyer leaves a package: Iris Vale's diary, last entry dated three days after witnesses saw her drown. The beat is quiet competence shadowed by unease.

chapters.title: Entries After the End
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Reading the diary, Wren finds entries written in a different hand after Iris's supposed death—calm, deliberate, addressed to whoever might read them. He cross-references dates with dispatch logs and realizes someone was driving her routes after she vanished. The emotional beat is the thrill of an impossible clue.

chapters.title: The Sister Who Drowned First
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Digging into Iris's past, Wren learns her sister Nell died five years ago in a crash ruled accidental, with developer Cassian Roe's company named in sealed civil suits. The diary hints Iris believed Roe killed Nell. The beat is cold anger hardening into purpose.

chapters.title: Night Routes
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, with intercut diary excerpts from Iris. Wren maps the posthumous diary entries onto taxi routes and identifies a driver, Odile, who picked up a fare matching Iris's description weeks after the drowning. Odile denies everything—but her hands shake. The beat is first contact with the conspiracy's fear.

chapters.title: What the Police Already Know
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A detective, Harrow, warns Wren off the case, revealing the department closed it fast at someone's request. Wren realizes the law itself is compromised. The beat is disillusionment—the moment justice inside the system stops being an option.

chapters.title: The Woman in the Safe House
chapters.summary: Iris's POV, first time. Iris watches Wren from a rented room above a laundromat, torn between staying dead and trusting the dispatcher who keeps asking questions that could get him killed. She decides to test him. The beat is loneliness sharpened into resolve.

chapters.title: A Fare to Nowhere
chapters.summary: Iris's POV. Iris hires Wren's own taxi line under a false name, riding in circles while probing what he knows. Wren, recognizing her voice from a voicemail on the diary's tape, says nothing—and lets her go. The beat is two watchers deciding, silently, to trust.

chapters.title: Confession in Fragments
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. In a parking garage, Iris tells Wren the truth: she staged her death because Roe's fixers found her, and she has spent months gathering evidence of Nell's murder. But her key witness—a mechanic who tampered the brakes—is missing. The beat is grief shared becomes alliance formed.

chapters.title: The Mechanic's Last Shift
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Hunting the mechanic, Wren finds his garage burned and a body too badly damaged for easy ID—officially the mechanic, but the dental records don't fit. Someone is erasing witnesses ahead of schedule. The beat is dread accelerating; the clock starts ticking loudly.

chapters.title: Harrow's Debt
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren confronts Detective Harrow, who confesses he buried Nell's case years ago under pressure and has hated himself since. He won't help officially, but slips Wren a file. The beat is a broken man choosing a small redemption.

chapters.title: Roe's City
chapters.summary: Iris's POV. Iris traces how Roe bought judges, alibis, and eventually her sister's silence, realizing her testimony alone will never survive his influence. She proposes something outside the courts entirely: a public confession, broadcast. The beat is strategy born of desperation.

chapters.title: The Tail
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren notices surveillance on his apartment and leads the fixers on a night-long chase through the taxi grid, using drivers as unwitting cover. He loses them but knows they've connected him to Iris. The beat is paranoia becoming intimacy with danger.

chapters.title: Odile Breaks
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Odile admits she ferried Iris for months out of guilt—she once drove Nell home the night she died and said nothing about the car following them. Her testimony fills the timeline. The beat is complicity confessed, forgiveness uncertain.

chapters.title: The Dead Witness Problem
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. To make a dead woman's testimony count, Wren plans to deliver Iris's recorded confession alongside proof she's alive—but revealing she's alive makes her a target again. They debate letting her stay dead forever versus justice. The beat is the book's moral crux laid bare.

chapters.title: Safe House Burning
chapters.summary: Iris's POV. Fixers find the laundromat room; Iris escapes through the roof minutes ahead of them, losing the original evidence cache except the diary. Wounded and furious, she calls Wren from a payphone. The beat is terror, then defiance—no more hiding.

chapters.title: Everything in One Night
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. With Harrow's file, Odile's statement, and the diary, Wren drafts the confession broadcast while Iris dictates her full account of Nell's death. Roe announces a memorial dedication for Iris—her own funeral exploited as PR. The beat is quiet fury assembling into a plan.

chapters.title: The Memorial
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. At the televised dedication, Wren infiltrates the venue's broadcast uplink while Iris, disguised among staff, prepares to appear alive on camera. Roe gives a eulogy praising the woman he hunted. The beat is coiled tension at its peak.

chapters.title: Witness
chapters.summary: Climax, alternating POV. The feed cuts to Iris's recorded confession naming Roe, synced with Harrow's file appearing on every screen in the hall. Roe's fixers move on Iris; Wren intervenes, taking a knife wound shielding her as cameras roll and Roe is arrested mid-eulogy. The beat is catharsis through exposure.

chapters.title: After the Cameras
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. In the hospital, Wren learns Roe's lawyers are already spinning, and some charges may not stick. Harrow resigns and hands over everything he kept hidden over the years. The beat is the sober truth that one night isn't the whole war.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Iris's POV. Months later, Iris testifies in open court, alive and named, as the diary is entered into evidence. Nell's case is reopened. The beat is grief given a public shape at last—memory honored by record.

chapters.title: Dispatch Closed
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren winds down his anonymous caseload, answering the last unanswered message on his board—an old missing person now found. He realizes invisibility was always a wound, not a skill. The beat is release.

chapters.title: Wren Thackeray, Present and Accounted For
chapters.summary: Final chapter, alternating POV. Wren and Iris meet at the river where she 'drowned.' He signs his real name to a statement helping prosecutors, stepping fully into the light; she begins writing a new diary, first entry addressed to him. The beat is identity reclaimed—witness and confessor, both finally seen.
